title: Why Some Faiths Avoid Images
objective: After this level you can explain why Judaism and Islam avoid images of God, and why Christians once fought over icons.
summary: Judaism and Islam avoid images of God, from the Second Commandment and the belief that God alone gives life. Byzantine Christians fought over icons for over a century before restoring them in 843.

cards.headline: Why would a faith refuse to picture the God it worships?
cards.body: Walk into a mosque and you'll find pattern and light, but no image of God. The reasons run deep, and among Christians they once divided an empire.

cards.headline: "Thou shalt not make"
cards.body: In the King James Version, Exodus 20:4 reads: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above." Its target, Britannica explains, was idol worship rather than art itself. Jewish art never vanished: the 3rd-century synagogue at Dura-Europos was painted with biblical scenes. What stayed off limits was an image to worship.

cards.headline: Islam: God alone gives life
cards.body: Muslims generally reject images of God and of the Prophet Muhammad, seeing them as a form of idolatry at odds with belief in one God. Behind the wider caution about picturing living beings lies the belief that God alone is the author of life, so a likeness can seem to rival him. In mosques, ornament took over: the endless arabesque is said to represent the infinite vastness of God.

cards.headline: When Christians fought over icons
cards.body: Christians argued too. From the 720s, Byzantine emperors, beginning with Leo III, attacked the veneration of icons as idolatry, citing the Ten Commandments. Defenders replied that images are symbols, that created matter has dignity, and that honor shown to an icon passes to the holy person it shows. After more than a century of struggle, Empress Theodora restored icons for good in 843.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: both sides opposed idolatry. They disagreed about whether honoring an icon is worshipping it.

cards.headline: Why Some Faiths Avoid Images: the takeaways
learned: The Second Commandment targets images made for worship
Muslims avoid images of God, believing God alone gives life
Byzantine Christians fought over icons until 843

questions.prompt: What did Empress Theodora do in 843?

options.label: Banned all icons in churches
options.rationale: Emperors like Leo III attacked icons; she restored them.

options.label: Moved the capital to Rome
options.rationale: That's unrelated to the icon dispute.

options.label: Wrote the Ten Commandments into law
options.rationale: Iconoclasts cited them; she ended iconoclasm.

questions.explanation: In 843 Empress Theodora restored the veneration of icons for good.

questions.prompt: Iconoclasts and icon defenders both rejected idolatry. What did they actually disagree about?

options.label: Which language to pray in
options.rationale: Nothing in the dispute was about language.

options.label: Whether honoring an icon is worship or passes to the person shown

questions.explanation: Iconoclasts saw icon veneration as idolatry; defenders said the honor passes to the holy person shown.

questions.prompt: Icons, painted synagogue walls and mosque arabesques all fall under which of Smart's dimensions from Level 3?

options.label: The doctrinal dimension
options.rationale: Doctrine is teaching; these are objects and art.

options.label: The social dimension
options.rationale: Social means the community and institutions.

options.label: The narrative dimension
options.rationale: Narrative is sacred story, though some art tells one.

questions.explanation: Smart's material dimension covers buildings and works of art.
